1.pericope_label: My heart’s desire for Israel: zeal without knowledge, and a righteousness of their own

schools.summary: Read the opening as a man clearing away suspicion before a sharper rebuke, straining to find some shadow of an excuse for those he must accuse; or as censure mingled with praise, the hook hidden beneath a bait so the benefit may be accepted; and take their own righteousness to be an unreasonable adherence to a law now ended.

Turn the verse on preachers, who take no pleasure in proclaiming that men are lost yet may sincerely seek the salvation of those they warn; quote Bengel that the prayer disproves absolute reprobation; correct the text, since Israel began as a marginal gloss; document the zeal from Josephus before criticising it; distinguish involuntary ignorance, which excuses, from ignorance bred of sin or indolence, which does not; and deny that the righteousness meant is the personal holiness of God rather than his plan of justifying men.

Add prudence to love as a motive, since neither Jews nor Gentiles would have received the teaching of a man they thought hostile; take the ignorance as a fact and destroy the excuse built on it, since those who crucified Christ had the very defence in which we confidently glory; distinguish three senses of God's righteousness and prefer the attribute of his justice; and make the two righteousnesses contraries, so that the first step toward his is to renounce our own.

Hold that they sinned more through ignorance than malice, which pleads in their excuse, and that the apology prepares them for harsher truths to come; argue that the prayer would not have been offered had they been absolutely reprobated; and compress the verse into an epigram against the reader — they had zeal without knowledge, we have knowledge without zeal.

Take the wish for their salvation to imply a wish for their conviction and conversion, since no one can pray in faith that men be saved in their unbelief, and observe that though the apostle preached against them he prayed for them.

debates: Why an apostle about to condemn his nation begins by professing love for it.
Whether the prayer for their salvation tells against absolute reprobation.
Whether ignorance lessens their guilt, and what kinds of ignorance excuse.
What the righteousness of God means here — his justice, his holiness, or his way of justifying.
outliers: Theodoret alone describes the praise as a bait concealing a hook.
Calvin alone uses their good intentions to abolish the excuse of good intentions generally.
Wesley and Bengel, quoted by Robertson, independently make the prayer an argument against absolute reprobation.
Ellicott alone reports that the name Israel entered the text from a marginal gloss.
Barnes alone calls the doctrine he had himself been defending appalling.

4.pericope_label: Christ the end of the law, and the righteousness of faith speaking in the words of Moses

schools.summary: Take end in the sense of termination, Christ superseding the law which then troubles a man no more, or else as the design and object had in view; or refuse to reduce the word, listing the stopping, the goal and the fulfilment together; concede that the words of Moses had quite another application and are used allegorically, or that the apostle borrows phrases without claiming Moses meant them, or that Moses nowhere described justification by faith but used language fitly expressing it; and correct the reading of the clause about living by them.

Set out five recognised senses of the word with their references and rule that the meaning depends on what it is joined to, calling Christ the law's perfection or landing-place; state the difficulty of the quotation without softening it, and untie it by showing that a law set before the eyes is no easier to keep than one far off, so Moses must have meant more than the law; and grant that Christ was the end of the ceremonial law in many respects without making that the chief sense.

Make the word mean the scope and aim of the law, whose very design is to bring men to believe; say that where the law ends Christ begins, the one closing with representative sacrifices and the other opening with the real offering; state that only he who keeps every precept in every point may claim life, which is impossible to any who has transgressed once; and suggest that those refusing Christ crucified must in effect be seeking another Messiah with a different revelation.

Deny that faith is contrary to the law, since the law itself directed us to Christ, so that whoever trusts him fulfils its intention; solve the difficulty of the quotation by changing the speaker, since it is God through Moses and not Moses himself who speaks; and take the descent into the deep for the resurrection, marshalling its witnesses by number.

Bring the passage to the point of use: it is not Christ in heaven nor Christ in the deep that is meant, but Christ in the promise, offered in the word, and no faith justifies which is not powerful in sanctifying the heart.

debates: Whether Christ is called the end of the law as its termination, its purpose, or in several senses at once.
How words spoken by Moses of the law may be applied by the apostle to faith.
Whether the righteousness of faith is here personified, and who is speaking.
What the law's own promise of life to the doer establishes.
outliers: Ellicott alone quotes Bengel's figure of the law ceasing to pursue a man who has reached his asylum.
Calvin alone enumerates five senses of the disputed word and derives a rule for choosing among them.
Robertson alone denies outright that Moses is being quoted as saying or meaning this.
Theodoret alone resolves the difficulty by making God rather than Moses the speaker.
Calvin alone argues that mere nearness of an unkeepable law would make the reasoning of Moses frivolous.

7.pericope_label: Who shall descend into the deep: the word nigh thee, and confession with the mouth

schools.summary: Show that the apostle has altered the question, since the Hebrew asks who shall cross the sea and he asks who shall descend into the abyss, and explain how formidable that crossing once was; credit the change to an orator's instinct rather than to quotation; dissolve the inverted order of mouth and heart by Hebrew parallelism, in which balanced clauses are equivalent; claim this as the earliest formal confession of faith on record; explain why the title Lord tests both Jew and Gentile; and give the resurrection the cardinal place, since without it the proof of Messiahship would be incomplete.

Say without embarrassment that God spoke the words concerning the law and the apostle has transferred them to faith, so that what Moses once said of the law's injunctions we now say of believing, and warn against over-curious inquiry into the dispensation in Christ; and gather the texts that seat Christ at the right hand of God.

Contrast a righteousness that shows itself at a distance and so keeps men off with one that offers itself at hand and invites us, while adding that the limits of the word are prescribed lest men be led away by crafts; state the difficulty of confession being named before belief and offer two solutions, the order of Moses and the maxim that we know faith only by profession; and require the confession to be hearty, public, and grounded in experience of grace.

Take the nearness as comfort, there being no occasion to seek high or low since the way is plain and the doctrine easy to profess; reduce the whole to depending solely on him who died for our offences and rose for our justification; and note that the confession is required even in persecution, when it may send a man to the lions.

debates: Why the question about the sea has become a question about the abyss.
Whether the nearness of the word is only an invitation or also a boundary.
Why confession with the mouth is named before belief in the heart.
What weight the resurrection carries beside the death, and what the title Lord costs the one who uses it.
outliers: Barnes alone reconstructs how formidable a sea crossing was when the words were first written.
Robertson alone ascribes the alteration to rhetorical skill rather than to quotation.
Ellicott alone removes the difficulty of the order by appealing to Hebrew parallelism, and alone claims this as the earliest creed.
Robertson alone explains why the one title would be refused by an untrusting Jew and an unconverted Gentile alike.
Wesley alone names the lions.

10.pericope_label: Believing with the heart and confessing with the mouth: no difference between Jew and Greek

schools.summary: Note that the logical order of faith and confession is restored here after being inverted; deny that any faith is genuine which does not influence the whole mind; observe that the apostle has added the word every one to the prophet's indefinite saying; qualify the denial of difference as holding for justification rather than for every respect; and correct the construction so that the words over all belong to the Lord, who is Christ, and not to his riches.

Report that both verbs are impersonal, and two judgments on the pairing — that God knows our faith but men know it by confession, and that faith and confession are not to be assigned each to its own result but taken together as an antithesis; describe at length what believing is not before saying that it is heart work, a going out of the soul to Christ; argue the absence of difference from creation, since the Maker of the world is God of all and an infinite mercy must reach all who seek it; and explain why the Greek reads ashamed where the Hebrew reads make haste.

Divide the clauses, believing obtaining justification and confessing final salvation, the one the root of all inward and the other the whole of outward religion; require the heart to be duly affected with a sense of guilt and of the sufficiency of the sacrifice; observe that a grand object throughout is the simplicity of the gospel against a law full of ceremonies; and press the threefold repetition to imply that the will of God is that all should savingly call upon him.
State the equality from the character of God: there is not one God to the Jews who is more kind and another to the Gentiles who is less kind, but the same to all, a common father of mankind.
Require both a sound and firm faith and a confession uttered with boldness, that the heart may be adorned with persuasion and the tongue dignified with fearless proclamation of the truth.

debates: Whether faith and confession are two stages with distinct results or one antithesis to be taken together.
What believing with the heart consists in, and what it excludes.
What follows from the apostle adding the word every one to the prophet's saying.
On what ground the difference between Jew and Greek is denied.
outliers: Calvin alone reports an authority denying that righteousness and salvation are to be divided between faith and confession, which is precisely the division Wesley makes.
Robertson, Gill and Calvin independently notice the added word every one.
Calvin alone explains the divergence between the Greek and Hebrew readings of the prophet.
Ellicott alone reattaches the words over all to the Lord and identifies that Lord as Christ.
Wesley alone draws from the repetition that God wills all men to call upon him.

13.pericope_label: Whosoever shall call: the chain of preaching, sending, hearing and believing

schools.summary: Observe that a promise made in the Old Testament to Jehovah is here applied to Christ, one of many such transfers; reconstruct the objection as a Jew would put it, that salvation is made to depend on a faith the nation had no chance to reach; note that the apostle picks up each preceding verb to challenge it, making a powerful plea for missions; grant that the Jews themselves held a divine message must be borne by a commissioned messenger; and correct the quotation, since the clause about the gospel of peace is absent from the oldest manuscripts.

Take the chain as objection and answer, framed to convict the hearers and remove every excuse, since they were punishable for the ignorance itself; notice that the two quotations are fitted to the heart and to the tongue of the preceding verses; observe that the order runs backwards, the sending of preachers being first in time and last in the argument, and that positions laid down as if to vindicate the Jews in fact increase their blame; and press the doubled Lord of the theophany as a covert teaching of Father and Son.

Read the passage as a constructive ladder in beautifully graduated order — no salvation without the gospel, no gospel without preaching, no effectual preaching without a divine mission, no benefit unless it is heard; report the suggestion that feet in scripture stand for the principles a man acts on, so that these signify the validity of the messengers' commission; and keep the figure literal, of their very footsteps.

Divide the mission into the extraordinary kind the apostles had and the ordinary call of pastors, warning that the inward call does not arise from vanity or desire of applause; decline the question of lawful calling as beside the purpose here, and state instead that the gospel does not fall like rain from the clouds but is brought by the hands of men; and hold that a nation favoured with preaching has in that fact a pledge of divine love.

debates: Why a promise spoken of the Lord in the prophet is applied to Christ.
What the chain of questions is for — convicting the hearers, building an argument, pleading for missions, or defending the apostle's own commission.
Why the order of the chain runs backwards from what happens first.
What kind of sending is required of a preacher.
outliers: Theodoret alone matches the two quotations to the heart and the tongue of the preceding verses.
Clarke alone reads the chain upward as a graduated construction rather than as objections met.
Theodoret alone points out that the argument reverses the order of time, and that a vindication becomes an indictment.
Calvin alone finds the apostle defending his own ministry, which stood or fell with the calling of the Gentiles.
Calvin alone refuses the question of ministerial calling as beside the purpose, and answers it with a figure about rain.

16.pericope_label: They have not all obeyed: faith by hearing, and the sound gone out into all the earth

schools.summary: Confess that the connexion is not easy, and decide that the sixteenth verse is an admission by the apostle while the seventeenth is the objector's own turning of the quotation back on him; or explain the roughness as interleaving, the apostle beginning a second topic before finishing the first, so the verses reach forward and back past one another; note that report and hearing render one Greek word with a shift of reference; correct the reading to the word of Christ, taken as the word about him; and admit that the psalm quoted spoke of the testimony of the heavenly bodies.

Use the general disobedience to block an inference, since Israel had never been without the word and might boast if faith always followed it — many are called who are not chosen; hold that preaching produces faith and yet of itself avails nothing, becoming the instrument of God's power only when it pleases him to work, since the voice of man cannot penetrate the soul; admit frankly that the psalm quoted seems to bear little on the subject, speaking of the material works of God and not of apostles; and call preachers instruments only.

Hold that God brings the message but does not oblige men to embrace it, so that it saves only if affectionately credited; guard the rule that faith comes by hearing with the word ordinarily; and carry the psalm by analogy, since as the luminaries testified of the eternal power and Godhead to the habitable world, so the gospel has testified through Palestine and the whole empire.

Argue from the order of the mission that the Jews cannot have failed to hear, since the nations of the whole earth had heard and the preachers came to them first; and rebuke the objectors sharply, bidding them read Lamentations and setting believing Persians against unbelieving Hebrews.

Observe that the time of God's patience is called a day, fit for work but limited as a day with a night at the end of it, and that we may wonder as much at a mercy not overcome by man's badness as at a badness not overcome by God's goodness.

debates: Whose voice speaks the words that faith comes by hearing — the apostle's or the objector's.
Why the argument of the chapter does not run straight at this point.
Whether preaching produces faith of itself, by divine working, or only when it is credited.
How a psalm about the testimony of the heavens can be applied to the preachers of the gospel.
outliers: Barnes alone reassigns a verse of the chapter to the objector rather than to the apostle.
Ellicott alone maps the disorder as two arguments interleaved, each reaching past the other.
Calvin alone draws the distinction between the called and the chosen out of this verse, to forestall a boast.
Clarke and Calvin state opposite doctrines of the same verse, one making the word effectual only when credited and the other only when God works.
Wesley alone guards the rule about hearing with the word ordinarily.

19.pericope_label: Moses and Isaiah on the calling of the Gentiles and the disobedience of Israel

schools.summary: Note that the apostle does not say what Israel knew, leaving it to be gathered from what follows; read the prophecy of jealousy as an exact requital, favour to a no-nation answering the worship of no-gods, and explain the terms as Jewish usage about neighbours; take first to mean earliest in time and in scripture; gloss the prophet's boldness as daring in the face of danger; and state without flinching that the words applied to the Gentiles referred originally to apostate Israel, and that the following words come from the next verse of the same prophecy, where no such distinction of persons is drawn.

Turn the question into an objection from the less to the greater, since aliens run to a light shown from afar while the race of Abraham rejects it seen at home; allow that Israel knew the gospel nationally and speculatively and rejected it against conviction; read the prophet's boldness as plainness of speech rather than bravery; and answer the difficulty of the two quotations by showing they stand connected in the prophet, where the turning to the Gentiles has the perverseness of Israel subjoined as its reason.

State the symmetry of the requital, that those who provoked with no-gods are provoked by a no-people; gather the argument of the chapter, that Jewish unbelief was their own obstinacy, was foretold seven centuries before, and so far from proving the gospel insufficient proves it the means God provided; and close by matching the disobedient and gainsaying people against those who believe with the heart and confess with the mouth.

Take the name foolish to oneself, since it is we who laboured under that folly before our conversion, as the apostle confessed of himself; observe that neither captivity nor dispersion nor the loss of the temple has grieved the Jews as the eminence of the Gentiles has; and read the phrase all day long as without ceasing, on the authority of two Greek versions.

debates: What it was that Israel is charged with knowing.
How the prophecy of provoking to jealousy answers the sin it punishes.
Whether the prophet's boldness lay in his courage or in his plainness.
How words spoken in the prophet of Israel come to be applied to the Gentiles, and whether the contrast drawn is in the original.
outliers: Theodoret alone applies the word foolish to himself and his own people rather than to others.
Calvin alone reads the prophet's boldness as plainness of speech rather than as courage under danger.
Ellicott alone states plainly that the quotation used of the Gentiles was spoken of Israel, and that the contrast between the two quotations is not in the prophet.
Calvin alone answers that difficulty by showing the two sentences stand connected in the original and are reversed in the citation.
Wesley alone closes the chapter by setting its last verse against its tenth.
